column1: # Local additions to the vendored word list, in the same TSV format:
# Lines starting with '#' and blank lines are ignored.
# Entries here override words.tsv when keys collide.
# Keep to spellings that are unambiguously wrong in American technical prose.
# Do not add register/dialect swaps that change meaning or tone.
# DO NOT EXTEND THIS LIST BY SUFFIX RULE. Add words one at a time, by hand.
# It is tempting to generate entries with a rule like -ise -> -ize or
# -lled -> -led. Both have almost no signal. Measured over one real 330-file
#                             English, ZERO British verb forms. advertise,
# A naive -ise pass over that corpus would corrupt 324 correct words to fix 0.
# A naive double-l pass, 577 to fix 0.
# The discriminator is etymological and prosodic, not orthographic. -ise is a
# British verb ending but also the ordinary ending of French-derived nouns.
# Double-l before a suffix is correct American when the stress falls on the
# final syllable (control -> controlled) and British only when it does not
# (label -> labelled). No suffix rule can see stress or etymology.
# The one rule that is safe is the prefix resolution in the script, and only
# because it composes a KNOWN-good pair with a prefix: the etymology question
# is already settled by a human having put the stem on the list.
# SCOPE OF THOSE NUMBERS: one author, one technical domain, and the -ise
# population there is dominated by real-estate and GIS vocabulary. The shape of
# the result should generalize -- these suffixes carry little signal anywhere --
# but the counts should not be inherited. Anyone working a medical, legal or
# literary corpus should re-measure rather than quote these figures.
